title: Section 1.3: Adding & Subtracting Polynomials — Key Terms
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 (Workbook p. 12)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Polynomial Terminology (Workbook p. 12)
- **Polynomial:** A monomial, or two or more monomials combined by addition or subtraction.
- **Monomial:** Exactly one term ($7x^2$, $-5$).
- **Binomial:** Exactly two terms ($3x + 4$, $y^2 - 9$).
- **Trinomial:** Exactly three terms ($ax^2 + bx + c$).
- **Like Terms:** Terms having the **exact same variable(s) and exponent(s)**. Only coefficients are added/subtracted.
pitfall: **Sora's Warning:** When adding like terms, NEVER add or change the exponents! $3x^2 + 5x^2 = 8x^2$, NOT $8x^4$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 07 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the desk is TA Sora. Today, we open Section 1.3 of our course workbook, found on page 12: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials. Hello everyone!

[TA Sora] Today we transition from working with single-term monomials to working with polynomialsâexpressions that contain multiple terms combined by addition and subtraction.

[Prof. Park] In the real world, polynomials are the mathematical models behind everything from cost and revenue curves in business, to trajectory curves of aircraft landing at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport, to stress loads on construction framing in Gallatin Valley residential builds.

[TA Sora] For example, a business in Belgrade might model its total revenue as R(x) = 150x - 0.5x^2, and its production costs as C(x) = 3000 + 40x. To find profit, they subtract the cost polynomial from the revenue polynomial: P(x) = R(x) - C(x)!

[Prof. Park] Understanding how to classify, add, subtract, and distribute polynomials is the foundational engine of business, engineering, and data science. Let's review the essential vocabulary on slide 1: A monomial has exactly 1 term (like 5x^3). A binomial has exactly 2 terms (like 2x + 7).

[TA Sora] A trinomial has exactly 3 terms (like 4x^2 - 5x + 9). And any algebraic expression composed of one or more terms is a polynomial. Each term consists of a numerical coefficient and variable factors.

[Prof. Park] The degree of a single term is the sum of the exponents on its variables: for instance, 4x^3 has degree 3, while 7x^2 y^4 has degree 2 + 4 = 6! The degree of an entire polynomial is the highest degree of any term present.

[TA Sora] Sora, what is the golden requirement for combining terms in a polynomial? LIKE TERMS ONLY! Two terms are 'like terms' if and only if they have the exact same variable raised to the exact same exponent! For example, 5x^2 and 3x^2 are like terms because both have x squared.

[Prof. Park] But 5x^2 and 5x are NOT like terms because one has power 2 and the other has power 1. When you combine like terms, you add or subtract the numerical coefficients, and the variable part remains completely unchanged. Let's practice on slide 2!

title: Example 1A & 1B: Combining Like Terms
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 Example 1A & 1B (Workbook p. 12)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Simplify the polynomial by combining like terms (Workbook p. 12)
$$\text{A. } 6y + 12 - 7y$$
$$\text{B. } 9m^2 - 24m + 12m - 32$$
pitfall: **Sora's Watch-out:** In Part B, $9m^2$ has exponent 2, while $-24m$ has exponent 1. They are NOT like terms! Do not combine them into $-15m$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Let's examine Section 1.3 Examples 1A and 1B on workbook page 12: Part A: Simplify 6y + 12 - 7y. Part B: Simplify -3x^2 + 5x + 9x^2 - 2. In Part A, we have three terms: 6y, +12, and -7y.

[TA Sora] Let's identify the like terms: 6y and -7y both have the variable y to the first power. The constant 12 is on its own. Combine the like terms by adding their numerical coefficients: 6 - 7 = -1.

[Prof. Park] So 6y - 7y = -1y, which in algebra we write simply as -y. Now bring along the constant +12: our simplified expression is -y + 12 (or 12 - y). Notice how the variable y didn't change at allâit did not become y squared, and it did not disappear.

[TA Sora] Only the count of how many y's we have changed from 6 and -7 to -1. Now look at Part B: -3x^2 + 5x + 9x^2 - 2. Here we have terms of degree 2, degree 1, and degree 0 (the constant).

[Prof. Park] Let's group the degree 2 terms: -3x^2 and +9x^2. Combine their coefficients: -3 + 9 = +6, so we have 6x^2. Now look for other degree 1 terms: we have +5x, but no other x terms to combine with, so it stays +5x.

[TA Sora] And the constant -2 is alone, so it stays -2. Assembling in descending order of exponents gives: 6x^2 + 5x - 2. Why do we write it in descending order? Writing polynomials in descending degree orderâhighest power first, down to the constantâis standard mathematical etiquette.

[Prof. Park] It makes it easy to identify the leading coefficient, which is 6, the degree of the polynomial, which is 2 (a quadratic trinomial), and ensures everyone grading your paper can immediately confirm your answer.

[TA Sora] You can also align them in vertical columns on your paper: place degree 2 terms in one column, degree 1 in the next, and constants at the end, just like multi-digit addition in grade school!

title: Example 1C & 1D: Multi-Term Polynomial Simplification
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 Example 1C & 1D (Workbook p. 12)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Simplify the polynomial by combining like terms (Workbook p. 12)
$$\text{C. } 3n^2 - 17n - n^2 + 4n$$
$$\text{D. } 5x^3 + 3x^2 - 2x - 9 - 12x^3 - 10x + 4$$
pitfall: **Sign Error Alert:** Don't forget that $-n^2$ means $-1n^2$. So $3n^2 - 1n^2 = 2n^2$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Moving to slide 3, let's tackle Examples 1C and 1D: Part C: 3n^2 - 17n - n^2 + 4n. Part D: 4ab^2 + 6a^2 b - 8ab^2 + 2a^2 b. In Part C, notice the term -n^2.

[TA Sora] Whenever a variable appears with a negative sign but no written number in front, its invisible coefficient is 1! So -n^2 is really -1n^2. Always write that little '1' with your pencil if you are prone to skipping it.

[Prof. Park] Now let's group the n^2 terms: 3n^2 - 1n^2 = (3 - 1)n^2 = 2n^2. Next, group the linear n terms: -17n + 4n = (-17 + 4)n = -13n. Combine them: 2n^2 - 13n.

[TA Sora] Students often ask: 'Can I combine 2n^2 - 13n into -11n?' Absolutely not! n^2 and n are completely different dimensionsâone is an area of size n by n, and the other is a length of size n. They cannot be combined!

[Prof. Park] Now look at Part Dâthis is a classic exam trap: 4ab^2 + 6a^2 b - 8ab^2 + 2a^2 b. Sora, both terms contain a and b, so why aren't all four of them like terms? Because the exponents on the individual variables are different!

[TA Sora] In 4ab^2, the b is squared: a^1 b^2. In 6a^2 b, the a is squared: a^2 b^1. Think of construction materials: ab^2 is a board of width a and length b squared, while a^2 b is a board of width a squared and length b!

[Prof. Park] They have different geometric shapes and cannot be stacked together. Let's combine matching categories: For the ab^2 group: 4ab^2 - 8ab^2 = (4 - 8)ab^2 = -4ab^2. For the a^2 b group: 6a^2 b + 2a^2 b = (6 + 2)a^2 b = +8a^2 b.

[TA Sora] Our final answer is: -4ab^2 + 8a^2 b (or 8a^2 b - 4ab^2). Always match the exponent to the specific letter!

title: Example 2A & 2B: Adding & Subtracting Polynomial Groups
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 Example 2A & 2B (Workbook p. 12)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Perform the indicated operation and simplify (Workbook p. 12)
$$\text{A. } (5x^3 + 2x^2 - 13x) + (4x^3 - 10x^2 + 9)$$
$$\text{B. } (2y^6 + y^4 - y) - (8y^6 - 3y^4 + 9y)$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ A\ (Addition):}\quad & (5x^3 + 4x^3) + (2x^2 - 10x^2) - 13x + 9 \\
&= \mathbf{9x^3 - 8x^2 - 13x + 9} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ B\ (Subtraction):}\quad & \text{Distribute the negative sign to every term in 2nd group!} \\
&= 2y^6 + y^4 - y - 8y^6 + 3y^4 - 9y \\
&= (2y^6 - 8y^6) + (y^4 + 3y^4) + (-y - 9y) \\
&= \mathbf{-6y^6 + 4y^4 - 10y}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **THE BIGGEST EXAM TRAP IN 1.3:** In Part B, distribute the minus to all terms! $-(8y^6 - 3y^4 + 9y) = -8y^6 + 3y^4 - 9y$. Watch the $+3y^4$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 4 takes us to Example 2 Parts A and B on page 12: Adding and Subtracting Polynomial Groups: Part A: (5x^3 + 2x^2 - 13x) + (4x^3 - 8x^2 + 2x). Part B: (7x^2 - 5x + 3) - (2x^2 - 9x - 6).

[TA Sora] In Part A, we are ADDING two polynomial groups. When there is an addition sign (+) between the parentheses, the parentheses serve only as containers and can simply be removed without altering any signs! Let's remove the parentheses and group like terms: Cubic terms: 5x^3 + 4x^3 = 9x^3.

[Prof. Park] Quadratic terms: 2x^2 - 8x^2 = -6x^2. Linear terms: -13x + 2x = -11x. Our resulting polynomial is: 9x^3 - 6x^2 - 11x. But in Part B, we have SUBTRACTION: (7x^2 - 5x + 3) - (2x^2 - 9x - 6).

[TA Sora] Sora, what is the single biggest trap on algebra exams with polynomial subtraction? Students only subtract the very first term, 2x^2, and leave the other terms untouched! That minus sign sitting outside the second parentheses acts as a multiplier of negative 1: -1 Â· (2x^2 - 9x - 6).

[Prof. Park] It MUST distribute to EVERY single term inside that second set of parentheses! Watch what happens to the signs: - (2x^2) becomes -2x^2. - (-9x) becomes +9x! The negative times negative becomes positive! - (-6) becomes +6! The negative times negative becomes positive!

[TA Sora] Rewrite the entire line without parentheses: 7x^2 - 5x + 3 - 2x^2 + 9x + 6. Now combine like terms: 7x^2 - 2x^2 = 5x^2. -5x + 9x = +4x. +3 + 6 = +9. Our final simplified result is: 5x^2 + 4x + 9!

[Prof. Park] Distributing that negative sign across all three terms is the secret to 100% accuracy on subtraction problems.

[TA Sora] If you have time, you can even check your answer by adding the result (5x^2 + 4x + 9) back to the subtracted group (2x^2 - 9x - 6) to verify it yields the original (7x^2 - 5x + 3)!

title: Example 3A & 3B: Distributive Property with Monomials
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 Example 3A & 3B (Workbook p. 13)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Perform the indicated operations and simplify fully (Workbook p. 13)
$$\text{A. } -2x(3x^2 + 8x - 4)$$
$$\text{B. } 2(8y - 5) + 7(-2y - 6)$$
pitfall: **Negative Monomial Multiplication:** In 3A, $(-2x)(-4) = +8x$. A negative times a negative is POSITIVE!
script:
[Prof. Park] Now let's explore the Distributive Property with Monomials on slide 5: Examples 3A and 3B on workbook page 13: Part A: -2x(3x^2 + 8x - 4). Part B: 4x^2(2x^3 - 5x + 7). The Distributive Property says: a(b + c + d) = ab + ac + ad.

[TA Sora] The monomial sitting outside multiplies every single term inside the parentheses! Think of a physical rectangular field in Gallatin County partitioned into three sections: the common width is -2x, and the three lengths are 3x^2, 8x, and -4. The total area is the sum of the three individual section areas!

[Prof. Park] And remember: when multiplying variable terms, we use the product rule from Lecture 05âwe MULTIPLY the coefficients and we ADD the exponents! Let's distribute -2x to each of the three terms in Part A: First term: (-2x)(3x^2). Multiply coefficients: -2 Â· 3 = -6.

[TA Sora] Add exponents: x^1 Â· x^2 = x^3. Result: -6x^3. Second term: (-2x)(8x). Multiply coefficients: -2 Â· 8 = -16. Add exponents: x^1 Â· x^1 = x^2. Result: -16x^2. Third term: (-2x)(-4). Negative times negative is positive! (-2)(-4) = +8, with x attached: +8x.

[Prof. Park] Assemble the three products: -6x^3 - 16x^2 + 8x. Notice the signs flipped completely: positive 3x^2 became negative, positive 8x became negative, and negative 4 became positive! Now let's do Part B: 4x^2(2x^3 - 5x + 7). Term 1: (4x^2)(2x^3) = (4 Â· 2) x^(2 + 3) = 8x^5.

[TA Sora] Term 2: (4x^2)(-5x^1) = (4 Â· -5) x^(2 + 1) = -20x^3. Term 3: (4x^2)(7) = (4 Â· 7) x^2 = +28x^2. Combine them: 8x^5 - 20x^3 + 28x^2. Notice that there are no like terms among x^5, x^3, and x^2, so this polynomial is fully simplified.

[Prof. Park] Think of residential construction framing across Bozeman and Belgrade: when contractors calculate structural perimeter lumber or roof truss dimensions with varying spans, variables represent modular lumber dimensions. Missing terms just mean zero length in that specific componentâthey do not vanish or break the formula!

[TA Sora] That is why I tell students to write in placeholder zeros if it helps them stay aligned on paper: write + 0x^3 as a placeholder column. That way, degree 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0 terms line up in neat vertical columns like an accounting ledger!

title: Example 3C & 3D: Higher Degree Distribution
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 Example 3C & 3D (Workbook p. 13)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Perform the indicated operations and simplify fully (Workbook p. 13)
$$\text{C. } -x(x^2 - 4) - 2(x^3 + 2x)$$
$$\text{D. } y(7y^2 + 4y - 9) - 3(8y^3 - 3y^2 - 4y)$$
pitfall: **Notice Cancellation in 3C:** $4x - 4x = 0$. The linear terms completely cancel out!
script:
[Prof. Park] Moving to slide 6, let's examine Examples 3C and 3D: Part C: -x(x^2 - 4) - 2(x^3 + 2x - 5). Part D: 3x^2(x - 4) + 2x(x^2 - 5x + 1). In Part C, we have TWO separate distributive blocks separated by subtraction: Block 1: -x(x^2 - 4).

[TA Sora] Distribute -x: (-x)(x^2) = -x^3, and (-x)(-4) = +4x. Block 2: -2(x^3 + 2x - 5). Distribute -2: (-2)(x^3) = -2x^3, (-2)(2x) = -4x, and (-2)(-5) = +10. Now write all terms in a single line and combine like terms: -x^3 + 4x - 2x^3 - 4x + 10.

[Prof. Park] Cubic terms: -1x^3 - 2x^3 = -3x^3. Linear terms: +4x - 4x = 0x! They cancel each other out completely! Constant: +10. So our simplified result is simply: -3x^3 + 10! Now let's conquer Part D: 3x^2(x - 4) + 2x(x^2 - 5x + 1).

[TA Sora] Distribute the first block: 3x^2(x) - 3x^2(4) = 3x^3 - 12x^2. Distribute the second block: 2x(x^2) - 2x(5x) + 2x(1) = 2x^3 - 10x^2 + 2x. Now combine like terms: Cubic terms: 3x^3 + 2x^3 = 5x^3. Quadratic terms: -12x^2 - 10x^2 = -22x^2. Linear term: +2x.

[Prof. Park] Final polynomial: 5x^3 - 22x^2 + 2x. Modularity makes even long problems simple. Multi-variable polynomials appear constantly in physics, such as calculating kinetic energy or heat dissipation across rectangular panels where length x and width y both vary simultaneously.

[TA Sora] And notice the order in each term: by mathematical convention, we write variable factors in alphabetical order: x before y, a before b. This makes spotting like terms instantaneous!

title: Example 3E & 3F: Nested Parentheses Simplification
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 07 • Section 1.3 Example 3E & 3F (Workbook p. 13)
detail: Lecture 07: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials & The Distributive Property
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Simplify fully by clearing nested grouping symbols (Workbook p. 13)
$$\text{E. } 3 + 2(5x - 4(x - 9)) + 7x$$
$$\text{F. } 11x - 8(y + 5(y - 2(y - x)))$$
pitfall: **Order of Operations:** In 3E, NEVER add $3 + 2 = 5$ at the start! Multiplication takes precedence over addition!
script:
[Prof. Park] To conclude Lecture 07, let's look at slide 7: Nested Grouping SymbolsâExamples 3E and 3F: Part E: 3 + 2[ 5x - 4(x - 9) ] + 7. Sora, when grouping symbols are nested inside brackets, how do we proceed? Work strictly from the INSIDE OUT!

[TA Sora] Always locate the innermost parentheses first. Here, the innermost part is -4(x - 9). Distribute -4: (-4)(x) = -4x, and (-4)(-9) = +36. Now look inside the brackets: [ 5x - 4x + 36 ]. Combine like terms inside the brackets: 5x - 4x = x.

[Prof. Park] So the brackets collapse to [ x + 36 ]! Look how clean that is! Now our expression is: 3 + 2[ x + 36 ] + 7. Next, distribute the outside 2 into the brackets: 2(x) = 2x, and 2(36) = 72.

[TA Sora] Now our full line is: 3 + 2x + 72 + 7. Now simply combine all the constants: 3 + 72 = 75, plus 7 = 82! So our final simplified answer is: 2x + 82.

[Prof. Park] Look at how an intimidating problem with brackets, parentheses, and four operations collapsed into a simple two-term binomial: 2x + 82! When students try to rush and distribute from the outside in, they create enormous fractions and sign errors. Working from the inside out guarantees clarity at every step.

[TA Sora] In Lecture 08, we advance to Section 1.4: Multiplying Polynomials and the FOIL Method on workbook page 14. Practice combining like terms tonight, and we will see you in Lecture 08! Let us emphasize one final time the difference between adding terms and multiplying terms:

[Prof. Park] When adding like terms: 3x^2 + 5x^2 = 8x^2. The coefficients add, but the exponent NEVER changes! When multiplying: (3x^2)(5x^2) = 15x^4. The coefficients multiply and the exponents ADD! Confusing these two rules is the number one cause of lost points on Exam 1!

[TA Sora] Take your time with every step here. Writing out intermediate lines is the secret to 100% accuracy!

[TA Sora] Exactly! Protect your signs, trust the algebra rules, and you will get the correct answer every single time!
